prompt: Which comment in a Java file does the `javadoc` tool turn into documentation?
hint: Count the asterisks, and look at where it sits.

choices.text: Any `/* */` comment, wherever it sits in the class
choices.why: A block comment with one asterisk is ignored, however much it says. The tool looks for `/**`.

choices.text: A `/**` comment directly in front of a declaration
choices.why: Right. Two asterisks, and immediately before the class, field, constructor or method it documents; annotations may sit between them.

choices.text: Every `//` line that ends with a full stop
choices.why: Line comments are never read by `javadoc`. They are notes for whoever edits the file.

choices.text: Any comment that contains an `@param` or `@return` tag
choices.why: Tags only mean something inside a Javadoc comment. In a `/* */` or `//` comment they are ordinary text.

prompt: After changing `@param q` to `@param query` in `BookController`, `mvn -q javadoc:javadoc` printed nothing at all. Why?
hint: Look at what the plugin keeps in `target` between runs.

choices.text: `-q` hides errors as well as information
choices.why: `-q` hides everything except errors. The same `-q` printed the error once `clean` was added.

choices.text: A wrong `@param` name is a warning, and warnings are not shown with `-q`
choices.why: It is an error, `error: @param name not found`, and it failed the build when the tool actually ran.

choices.text: Doclint only checks comments on classes, not on methods
choices.why: The error it reported was on line 48, inside the comment of the `search` method.

choices.text: The plugin saw an unchanged command line and skipped
choices.why: Right. Its stale-data file records the command line, not the sources, so an edited comment changes nothing it compares. `clean` removes the record.

prompt: `BookNotFoundException` is unchecked, so `get(long id)` does not declare it. The block tag that documents it in the comment is `@___`.
With `<doclint>all</doclint>`, doclint reported 92 elements with no comment, among them the handlers of `ApiErrorHandler` and the controller's constructor. What does `all,-missing` do about them?
hint: Read the minus sign as a subtraction from a list of check groups.

choices.text: Leaves them undocumented and still checks every comment that is written
choices.why: Right. Only the group that demands a comment everywhere is switched off; a wrong `@param` still fails the build.

choices.text: Hides them from the generated pages
choices.why: What goes in the pages is decided by `<show>public</show>`. Doclint checks comments and decides nothing about the pages.

choices.text: Writes a placeholder comment for each of them
choices.why: No tool here writes comments. Doclint only reports, and `-missing` makes it stop reporting one kind of thing.

choices.text: Turns the 92 warnings into errors, so the build fails until each is documented
choices.why: That is the opposite direction. The minus removes the `missing` group from `all`.

prompt: Your team publishes the ISBN check from `Isbn` as a small library on Maven Central, for other bookshops to use. What should change in its Javadoc configuration, compared with the bookshop's?
hint: Who reads a library's public methods, and how?

choices.text: Nothing: `-missing` is right for any project
choices.why: `-missing` is right where public methods are public only because a framework calls them. In a library, every public method is somebody's API.

choices.text: Turn the `missing` group back on, and publish a jar of the pages too
choices.why: Right. Other projects read a library through its Javadoc, so an undocumented public method is a defect there, and Central expects a javadoc jar beside the library.

choices.text: Use `<show>private</show>`, so users see how the check digit is computed
choices.why: Documenting private members invites users to depend on what you are free to change. The public contract is what they need.

choices.text: Add springdoc, because a library's users need an OpenAPI document
choices.why: OpenAPI describes an HTTP API. A library is called from Java, which is exactly Javadoc's reader.

prompt: With springdoc added and lesson 15's `SecurityConfig` unchanged, `GET /v3/api-docs` answered 401. Why?

choices.text: springdoc protects its document with a password of its own
choices.why: springdoc has no security of its own. The 401 came from the bookshop's filter chain, with a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` header.

choices.text: The document is only built after the first request that carries a valid token
choices.why: The same request without a token got the document as soon as its path was permitted.

choices.text: The application had not been rebuilt after the pom changed
choices.why: An unknown path is closed by the same `anyRequest().authenticated()`, so a 401 says nothing about the build. What fixed it was a rule.

choices.text: Every path the chain does not name falls to `anyRequest().authenticated()`
choices.why: Right. New paths are closed until somebody permits them, which is the safe default, and the fix was one `requestMatchers` line.

prompt: After `/v3/api-docs/**` was permitted, the document answered 200 but `/v3/api-docs.yaml` still answered 401. Why?

choices.text: springdoc serves YAML only to authenticated clients
choices.why: springdoc decides nothing about who may read. The 401 is the filter chain's.

choices.text: The pattern does not match `/v3/api-docs.yaml`
choices.why: Right. `/v3/api-docs/**` matches `/v3/api-docs` and the paths below it; `/v3/api-docs.yaml` is a sibling of the path, not a child, so it falls to `anyRequest().authenticated()`.

choices.text: YAML is disabled by default, and 401 is how a disabled endpoint answers
choices.why: A disabled endpoint answers 404, as the whole document did with `springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false`.

choices.text: The application had to be restarted a second time to serve the other format
choices.why: Both formats come from the same running application; a restart changes nothing about which paths the rule names.

prompt: Before any OpenAPI annotation was written, which of these did springdoc get right from the code alone? Choose all that apply.
hint: It reads mappings, parameter types, return types and the standard constraints.

choices.text: the 404 that `GET /books/{id}` gives for an unknown id
choices.why: The 404 comes from an exception and lesson 7's handler; the signature returns a `BookResponse`, and the first document listed a 200 only.

choices.text: `id` in `/books/{id}` as a required `integer` of format `int64`
choices.why: Right: `@PathVariable long id`, and a path variable cannot be left out.

choices.text: the 201 that `POST /orders` answers
choices.why: It said 200: the status is chosen at run time inside the method.

choices.text: `maxLength: 200` on the title of `BookRequest`
choices.why: Right, from `@Size(max = 200)`.

choices.text: that `POST /books` needs a token
choices.why: springdoc does not read the filter chain. No operation mentioned a token until `@SecurityRequirement`.

prompt: A client sends only requests that obey the `BookRequest` schema to the letter. Which one can still be refused with a 400?
hint: Which of the record's constraints has no JSON Schema keyword in the document?

choices.text: A book with `stock` 0
choices.why: `minimum: 0` allows 0, and so does `@PositiveOrZero`.

choices.text: A title of exactly 200 characters
choices.why: `maxLength: 200` and `@Size(max = 200)` both allow 200.

choices.text: A request with no `priceCents`
choices.why: That one does not obey the schema: `priceCents` is in `required`.

choices.text: Thirteen digits with a wrong check digit
choices.why: Right. `@ValidIsbn` is the bookshop's own constraint and springdoc does not know it, so the schema says only `string`.

prompt: `OrderController.place` answers 201, yet the generated document lists a 200 for `POST /orders`. Why?

choices.text: springdoc reads the declaration, and the status is chosen inside the method
choices.why: Right. `ResponseEntity<OrderResponse>` says nothing about which status; `ResponseEntity.created(...)` runs only when a request arrives.

choices.text: springdoc calls each operation once at start-up, and that call failed with no token
choices.why: springdoc never calls your methods. Placing an order would have changed the database.

choices.text: 201 is not a status OpenAPI can describe
choices.why: The final document lists a 201 for `POST /books`, declared with `@ApiResponse`.

choices.text: The order endpoints need a token, so springdoc could not inspect them
choices.why: It described them fully, path, body and schema. It reads the code, not the endpoints over HTTP.

prompt: Every method of `BookController` has a Javadoc comment, and springdoc used none of them. Why?
hint: What did `javap` find in the class file, and what did it not find?

choices.text: springdoc runs before `javadoc` in the build, so the pages do not exist yet
choices.why: springdoc does not run in the build at all; it runs inside the application, and it never reads HTML pages.

choices.text: springdoc ignores comments on purpose, so that the two documents stay apart
choices.why: It has no choice: by the time it runs, the comments are gone. Keeping them apart was this project's decision, not springdoc's.

choices.text: `javac` leaves comments out of the class file, and springdoc reads the running application
choices.why: Right. `grep -c` found the comment's words 0 times in `BookController.class`, and found the `summary` string twice.

choices.text: Only comments on classes reach springdoc, and the methods' are dropped
choices.why: The class's comment did not reach it either: the document's tag came from `@Tag`, not from the class comment.

prompt: Suppose the 404 on `get` were written `@ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "No book has that id")`, with no `content`. What would the document say a 404 carries?

choices.text: Nothing: a response with no `content` has no body
choices.why: springdoc fills in what was not declared, and it fills it from the method.

choices.text: A `ProblemDetail`, because springdoc reads `ApiErrorHandler`
choices.why: The `ProblemDetail` schema only appeared once `content` named it.

choices.text: A `BookResponse`, as `*/*`
choices.why: Right. Without `content`, every response gets the method's return type, which is a lie for an error.

choices.text: A plain-text message, the default for errors
choices.why: OpenAPI has no default for errors, and the bookshop's errors are JSON problem details.

prompt: Match each annotation to what it changes in the document.

pairs.right: the group the operations appear under
the one-line description of an operation
the operation needs the declared token scheme

right_distractors: which scope the token must carry

prompt: A client is generated from the final document, and reads the `errors` map of a 400 from the `properties` member of `ProblemDetail`. What happens when a validation fails?
hint: Compare the schema with the body lesson 7 printed.

choices.text: It finds the map there, since the document was generated from the real class
choices.why: Generated from the class, yes; but Jackson writes extra members at the top level, so the body and the class have different shapes.

choices.text: It finds nothing in `properties`: `errors` arrives beside `title` and `detail`
choices.why: Right. `properties` is the Java field that holds extra members, not a member of the JSON. The document describes the class rather than the wire.

choices.text: The bookshop answers 500, because the client's request carries a `properties` member
choices.why: The schema describes a response. Nothing a client reads changes what it sends.

choices.text: It cannot be generated at all, because `additionalProperties: {}` is invalid
choices.why: An empty schema is valid JSON Schema and means "anything". The problem is where the members are, not the syntax.

prompt: Where does Swagger UI get the operations it draws?

choices.text: From the controllers, which it scans in the jar
choices.why: Swagger UI is HTML and JavaScript in your browser. It knows only what the document says.

choices.text: From the document `swagger-config` names
choices.why: Right: `/v3/api-docs/swagger-config` answers `"url":"/v3/api-docs"`. A wrong document gives a wrong page.

choices.text: From the Javadoc pages in `target/reports/apidocs`
choices.why: Those pages are not in the jar and Swagger UI never reads them.

choices.text: From the requests it has seen the bookshop answer
choices.why: It sends requests only when you press Execute, and draws the operations before that.

prompt: The bookshop starts with `--springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false` and nothing else changed. What do `/v3/api-docs` and `/swagger-ui.html` answer?

choices.text: 404 and 200: the page loads and shows an error
choices.why: The page went too: `/swagger-ui.html` was a 404 as well.

choices.text: 401 for both, since they are no longer permitted
choices.why: The rule in `SecurityConfig` did not change. The paths are permitted and nothing answers at them.

choices.text: 404 for both
choices.why: Right. Swagger UI has nothing to draw without the document, so the one property switches off both, and the two warnings stop.

choices.text: Both still answer, because the warning said a second property is needed
choices.why: The second warning names a property for the page alone; switching off the document was enough for both.

prompt: To turn the document off from the environment rather than the command line, the bookshop is started with `___=false java -jar target/bookshop-0.1.0.jar`.
The search parameter was renamed from `q` to `text`. In code first, what noticed?

choices.text: The application, which refused to start with a changed contract
choices.why: It started without a word. There is no contract for it to compare against.

choices.text: springdoc, which printed a warning about a removed parameter
choices.why: springdoc describes the code as it is now and keeps no earlier version.

choices.text: Only a `diff` against the document saved before the change
choices.why: Right. One line changed in the document, and a client using `?q=` got a 400. A document kept in the repository makes that line show up in review.

choices.text: The compiler, because the Javadoc's `@param q` no longer matched
choices.why: The `sed` renamed the `@param` too, and the compiler never reads Javadoc anyway; doclint would have, but only when asked.

prompt: Put in order what it took for Swagger UI to show `POST /books` with a padlock and send it with a token.
hint: The document has to be reachable before anything can be added to it.
items: Permit `/v3/api-docs/**` and the Swagger UI paths in `apiChain`
Declare the `bearer` security scheme in the `OpenAPI` bean
Paste the clerk's token into the Authorize dialog
trap: Naming a scheme in `@Operation` before the `OpenAPI` bean declares it refers to a scheme that does not exist.

prompt: The order endpoints are still documented as springdoc inferred them. Which changes would make the document true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two things in it are false: a status, and the absence of a requirement.

choices.text: A Javadoc `@return` on `place` saying it answers 201
choices.why: Good for the Java reader, invisible to springdoc: the comment does not survive into the class file.

choices.text: `@ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", ...)` on `place`
choices.why: Right. The code answers 201, which springdoc cannot see in `ResponseEntity<OrderResponse>`.

choices.text: `@ParameterObject` on the `OrderRequest` parameter
choices.why: `OrderRequest` is a request body, already described as one. `@ParameterObject` is for an object read from the query string.

choices.text: A second security scheme called `orders`, to match the scope
choices.why: The orders take the same bearer token as the catalogue; a scheme says how a token is sent, not which scope it carries.

choices.text: `security = @SecurityRequirement(name = "bearer")` in the `@Operation` of both methods
choices.why: Right. Every order call needs a token, and the document cannot know that from the filter chain.

prompt: A partner needs the bookshop's OpenAPI document in production, and the team wants no Swagger UI there. Which of these keep the document and remove the page? Choose all that apply.
hint: Reread the second warning, and what the `-ui` in the starter's name brings.

choices.text: `springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false`
choices.why: Right. The second warning names this property for the page alone.

choices.text: `springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false`
choices.why: That removes the document too, and the partner gets a 404.

choices.text: Deleting `OpenApiConfig`
choices.why: The document would lose its title and its security scheme, and the page would stay.

choices.text: Depending on `springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-api` instead of the `-ui` starter
choices.why: Right. The `-ui` starter is the `-api` one plus Swagger UI; without it there is no page to serve.

prompt: Three companies will build mobile apps against a payments API your team has not written yet, and they start next month. Which approach fits, and why?

choices.text: Code first, because the document will always match the code
choices.why: It will, once the code exists. They start before it does, and a document that follows the code can change under them without anyone deciding to.

choices.text: Contract first: they need the document before the code exists
choices.why: Right. The contract is written and agreed first, they build against it, and the server is held to it by the generated interfaces.

choices.text: Javadoc, published on a website, because it is the most complete
choices.why: Javadoc describes Java classes. Mobile apps call HTTP, and they need paths, bodies and statuses.

choices.text: Swagger UI on the production server, so they can try each operation
choices.why: There is nothing to try before the API exists, and Swagger UI only draws a document that somebody has to write first.

prompt: If `list` were declared with `@PageableDefault(size = 50, sort = "id")`, what `default` would the final document give the `size` parameter?
hint: The document read 20 from the annotation as it is.
